speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: asked the Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (a) what is the current take-up rate by Malay/Muslims of the national financial and estate planning programmes available; (b) what are the current initiatives available to educate Malay/Muslims on permissible methods of investments and estate planning; and (c) what are the avenues for them to seek clarification or enquire about such financial or estate planning methods.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Under MoneySense, there are various initiatives, resources and tools to help Singaporeans make prudent decisions related to their savings, housing purchase, investments and retirement planning.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: First, MoneySENSE's website and social media channels provide free bite-sized information, starter packs and financial tools on financial planning.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Second, MoneySENSE offers free financial talks and workshops through the Institute for Financial Literacy (IFL).

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Since March this year, the IFL has been conducting periodic "Ask-Me-Anything" Facebook Live sessions, where individuals can ask trained finance professionals about topics such as estate planning and digital tools for financial planning.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In addition, MoneySENSE collaborates with various partners to reach out and provide financial education to Singaporeans at different stages of their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, MoneySENSE works with the Ministry of Social and Family Development to incorporate financial planning topics in the marriage preparation programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This includes Muslim couples attending the Cinta Abadi Marriage Preparation Programme, where they will learn how to plan ahead by making Central Provident Fund (CPF) nominations and the Lasting Power of Attorney.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Community initiatives supplement these national programmes to further strengthen support for the Malay/Muslim community, including newly wed couples and young families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MENDAKI SENSE’s Program Bijak Belanja engages young and low-income families to empower them with financial management skills.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The workshop is delivered in Malay and covers practical day-to-day management of family expenses.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Topics such as home ownership, basic investment and management of inheritance are also covered in the programme.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As part of the M3 initiative, the Naib Kadi or solemnisers will provide marital guidance to newly wed couples through the Bersamamu programme, so that they have a good start and build a strong foundation to their marriage.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Where required, the Naib Kadis will also refer couples to available community and national resources including financial support programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Financial planning courses will also be offered to newly wed couples and young Muslim families under Temasek Foundation's programme called "Achieving Resilient and Inspiring Families" or Project ARIF.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Religious guidance is also another way provided to the community on matters related to financial and estate planning tools.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MUIS has conducted seminars and talks on managing inheritance and organised several Continuous Professional Education or CPE training programmes on “Wealth and Estate Planning” for our asatizah.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: A free guidebook on the Islamic Law of Inheritance or what we call Faraidh, covering the financial and estate planning tools that can be practised by Muslims within Singapore’s context, is also accessible online.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The guidebook contains a helpful list of Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on managing inheritance.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In addition, MUIS has issued religious rulings or fatwas to guide the community in their estate planning and decision making.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Another one, the Joint Tenancy Fatwa permits the surviving joint tenant to have full ownership of the property, without the need for a transfer of ownership and being subjected to distribution of inheritance according to Islamic law.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And third, the CPF Nomination fatwa recognises the permissibility of the CPF nomination instrument.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Muslims can choose the CPF instrument or distribute their wealth according to faraidh, or exercise both options together.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The revenue generated through the investment of the Wakaf in capital-guaranteed instruments and properties is channelled towards supporting Islamic education in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My question is directed to the Minister for National Development.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First and foremost, I thank the Minister for that very nuanced exposition of the Ethnic Integration Policy (EIP).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think it has been the most nuanced reply that I have heard from a Government Minister on the EIP, considering on the one hand the realities of racial integration and other policies that can assist; and on the other, the fact that there are people who actually pay a price for the EIP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first pertains to the request for waivers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The numbers actually cascade lower in the years before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question is a question for information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 1989, when EIP was introduced, 28% of the neighbourhoods had already reached the established EIP guidelines on the start date of the EIP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Over the years, this has fallen but there is no real clarity about why this has fallen.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am specifically referring to the number of new neighbourhoods that have also come about.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the percentage can be very difficult to understand.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, in Kaki Bukit and Aljunied GRC, the neighbourhood level numbers for the Malay community are still, I believe, beyond the EIP limits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And there is nothing untoward about race relations in Kaki Bukit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I think this will be replicated in other parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, to this end, is the Government prepared to share details on the breakdown by ethnic groups in all HDB neighbourhoods, both new and old, on an annual basis from 1989?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If it is, then, we will file the question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is in view of the rising number of EIP waiver requests over the last few years, Singapore's changing demographic profile and for policy equity considerations towards communities that are adversely affected by the EIP.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, on the number of appeals from households from Indian or other ethnic origins, whether the review is ongoing, it continues to be so.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We look at the proportions of various ethnic groups over the years and we make adjustments, where necessary.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, 125 neighbourhoods then; 35 neighbourhoods reached one or more limits.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That is perhaps a result of a range of factors: the EIP operating, including operating in new neighbourhoods that are launched over the years since.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But also, a whole variety of factors: providing a whole range of flat types, providing for different budgets, programmes that promote a sense of belonging, programmes that help to integrate society together across races.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, a whole range of factors may have led to that.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As for rental flats, I recall reading in 2013, the Member asked, following a 2012 question he had asked to Minister Khaw Boon Wan, then Minister for National Development, and Minister Khaw said that for rental flats to accommodate the Malay households that are applying for rental housing, there would be an administrative 10-percentage point increment to accommodate.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Whether we will consider that across all housing types, as I said earlier, we are mindful of the intent of EIP as a bulwark against very strong socio-economic forces borne out of choices of individuals.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The EIP, we need to adjust along the way in terms of looking at proportions, but it is a very important bulwark.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, the question is how much more do you want to raise the cap?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In doing so, even when we allow appeals on a case-by-case basis, we are already pushing at the boundaries of what the policy seeks to achieve.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I looked at your manifestos and WP has said unequivocally from 2006 to last year, that WP wants the EIP to be abolished; and people should be able to stay wherever they want in our estates.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This would address the disadvantage faced by ethnic minority HDB flat resellers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Abolishing the quota will not cause racial disharmony amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: After more than 50 years of nation-building, our society has evolved and achieved multi-racial integration that has gone beyond the need for mandating proportionately mixed neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Singaporeans should therefore be given the freedom to choose where their homes will be without taking into account race." It is the same in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: You did not cite the impact on minority resellers but you say that society has now attained a level of multi-racial integration and therefore there is no longer a need for EIP.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In 2011, that is the same position except that in addition to saying that in 2011, Singapore had reached a high level of multi-racial integration and therefore there is no longer a need for people to be mandated to live with each other across different ethnicities in our neighbourhoods, WP goes on to say that the ethnic quota system also contradicts the policy of encouraging young families to live closer to their parents and prevent young Malay and Indian families from buying homes close to their parents.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I would dare say that also applies to Chinese families who are constrained by EIP even if they wish to live in the same block as their parents.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Between 1989 and 2006, we have no record of any position that WP has taken since the EIP was launched.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I looked at speeches made by the hon Leader of the Opposition as well as the Chairman of WP and other Members.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I just want to understand the rationale and, indeed, what the position is.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Because in the House, there has been no clear and unequivocal position taken by WP that you want the EIP abolished because you object to it and that Singapore has reached such a high level of multi-racialism that it is no longer necessary.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We, of course, take a very different view to that.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And the recent incidents over the years continue to remind us of the need to keep working at it and never rest on our laurels, that we can afford to take away mechanisms that are in place through the wisdom of the generations to keep our society where it is today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, I would like to seek some clarity.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Is it your position that there will not be racial concentrations if we abolish EIP?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Or are you saying that we have reached a level of multi-racial integration so that it does not matter if we have entire blocks and neighbourhoods of predominantly one race; society will not change if we have ethnic concentrations?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: What would your position be if you know that people go to the pre-schools, they go to the schools near their homes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And if we have neighbourhoods predominantly of one ethnic group, that will of course cascade into pre-schools, into our national school system.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The services in the heartlands, the shops, the markets, the hawker centre food choices, they will adjust to reflect the proportions of the clientele in the neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The availability of local jobs and the kinds of ethnic Singaporeans who fill those jobs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Yes, that is the Workers' Party (WP) position, as iterated by the Minister, in the manifesto.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It really is undergirded by the frustration that we sense from ethnic minorities who cannot sell their flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The question is: is the EIP the only policy, among a whole gamut of policies, that the Government has to encourage racial integration, bearing in mind that it is a pre-emptive policy introduced in 1989?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And we also have a hybrid system almost, in Singapore, where we do have places like Chinatown and Little India, where there are concentrations of a particular race but it does not disturb Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We may take a different philosophical approach as to what the end situation will be, but I cannot speculate on one or two episodes and say that because of that, we are descending in terms of our journey towards greater racial integration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My own sense on the philosophy behind the HDB EIP policy as it stands today – almost one generation since its introduction – is that it needs to be revisited.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It has to be revisited in the context and not limited to: number one, a larger national conversation on race relations in the context of today and tomorrow Singapore; and, separately, what it means to be Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Number two, the effect of immigration into Singapore from the 1990s after the EIP was introduced, leading to a larger Singapore family living in HDB flats that include communities outside the traditional CMIO categorisation such as naturalised Singaporeans from Myanmar, the Philippines and non-Tamil ethnic Indians.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Number three, the more common experience of mixed marriages amongst Singaporeans and separately between Singaporeans and non-Singaporeans, and its impact on traditional racial categorisations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That is shocking and that is really where we are coming from.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Number five and finally, a reassessment of Singapore's lived experiences which acknowledge policies and guidelines that have successfully encouraged racial integration such as national schools, anti-discrimination guidelines at the workplace, National Service, amongst others, and how these compare in today's time with the continued efficacy of the EIP as a policy tool of racial integration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The current policy as it stands has a larger impact on minorities, penalising them in the pocket when they have to sell their flat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: By minorities, I mean not just racial minorities, but those who are affected by it, including Chinese, Malays, Indians.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This may perversely interact with the stated objective of the policy of racial harmony, thereby breeding resentment amongst those who are affected by the policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For that reason, the EIP as it stands needs to be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We must always keep in focus the prospect of endeavouring towards a race-neutral society where race-based policies like the EIP are no longer needed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And just before I conclude, my second supplementary question was not just a general question about the percentages at a broad level.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, he says it is a pre-emptive policy in 1989.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If you look back in history and over the last few weeks and months as we continue to review our policies and preparing for today's session has been a humbling experience in learning from the wisdom of the generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A real pain in families grieving for lost loved ones and a country newly formed wrecked by racial riots and disharmony, distrust.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The efforts of HDB are not just to build homes for people who lived in slums and villages that flooded or were easily burned, but also ensuring that we learn those lessons, and in allocating new flats, make sure that in every block, there was a racial mix.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Taking people from what were ethnic enclaves, which were a legacy of the Jackson Plan and persisted through villages and enclaves of different races, pulling them up and saying, "You move into these high-rise homes in the sky, but we will mix you.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Learn to live with each other." If you talk to the earlier generation, it was not easy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I think today, there are still frictions along the way, but things have improved.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is not something that we decided to put in because we were looking at other countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We paid for it with the blood of our brethren and sisters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, the Member says that he or WP would like to abolish the EIP because of its disproportionate impact on minorities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I said earlier, the EIP has its rough edges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: By its very operation, it seeks to ensure that in every estate, from BTO all the way to resale flat, there is freedom to choose where you would like to live, subject to balloting or price.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But when it hits certain limits, and when the function of individual choices results in blocks exceeding significantly the demographic proportion of each ethnic group, then we have to kick in this bulwark and say, "Well, we will have to cap it".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Of course, it causes pain to minorities but also Chinese as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The proportion, of course, will be different because there are a lot more Chinese than there are the other ethnic minorities, and that is the reality of it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For Build-To-Order (BTO) applications in certain popular locations, say Bishan, Ang Mo Kio, you do have cases of Chinese coming up to say, "Look, I have been balloted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I have been asked to select, but the next day I am told sorry, EIP limit hit, and then the minority takes over my place".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we explain the rationale and seek their understanding, and by and large, all Singaporeans of all races have kept faith with the broader intent of this policy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But I accept the Member's point and I accept the point that was made by many Members of this House, both present and past, and looking at very thoughtful questions in speeches by both PAP Members and Members from across the aisle over the years, concerned about the impact on their constituents of all races, including minorities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And that is why we have been looking at it case-by-case, understanding the situation for each seller, looking at how long they have taken to market the flat, looking at the price if asked for, given the market conditions, and well, if today is EIP, tomorrow or next month, perhaps there might be a change of circumstances.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Or after a few months, the EIP may adjust because people buy and sell and the EIP may no longer apply to your block.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we look at it individually, bearing in mind that we have to be very judicious.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Otherwise, the lessons that we have learned will all unravel.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member talked about the case that the Chairman of WP sought to help and the example was raised twice as an anecdotal, but real, example of a person who lost $100,000 through resale.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Sylvia Lim's appeal to us was that the resident told her that she got offers for her flat that appeared to be $100,000 less than what other people nearby were offered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That was anecdotal, it was said to her.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I am not sure if the Member verified.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think better put these cases which are raised as anecdotal examples to rest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Having said that, there is impact, no doubt.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member, I am not sure whether he has addressed my question, but because of the impact on minorities, which we have said we address through appeals as well as through continuous smoothening of the rough edges, does he still take the position that we want to abolish the EIP for that reason?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if abolished, does WP believe that our estates will remain multicultural and representative?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I have also said earlier that there will be these knock-on effects, if whole estates become concentrated, to all these places, platforms and spaces that the Member talked about.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: From being common, they will be ethnic focused.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we will see what we can provide.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the point really, again, is the philosophy that we want to aim towards, towards a race-neutral society and we continue working towards this assiduously and keeping in mind that you do not want the policy to become a barrier to that vision, to that journey to become a race-neutral society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That is why we took the position that we had.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not believe the Minister has suggested what sort of policy beyond the very helpful clarification of the anecdote, I think this is how Parliament should work: if an example is brought up, the Government clarifies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, it is not as if the Government, the arguments that were made by the Minister for National Development are cast in stone.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If I have not answered any of the Minister's questions, please ask me again.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We take the position because we want to endeavour and move towards a race-neutral society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Those are details, important details but I think, fundamentally, it is important to understand, given the Government's position as articulated, that we continue to look at how we can smoothen the rough edges and given how over the last few years, we have started to see more appeals succeeding, do we recognise that that is on a case-by-case basis, providing a balm to a household but also not quite pushing the limits further.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if it abolishes, the important questions about your belief about what society will be like, I think that is most fundamental.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The other issues we can address, but we need to understand your position on multi-racialism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Number two, the importance of these bulwarks to ensure multi-racialism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Number three, your position on Chinese, Malays, Indians, Others (CMIO).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: You have talked about a race-blind society, a race-neutral, race-blind multicultural society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But yet over the years, we have been tracking; WP has been filing lots and lots of questions specific to individual minorities or races.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in fact, I understand Member Mr Faisal Manap had asked a PQ before, asking for assurances that we will ensure that the ethnic mix in Singapore will remain and wants to keep a very close eye on ethnic issues.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I just wanted to ask a clarification of the Leader of the Opposition because I was listening to his response.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think he had started out by saying that the EIP should be revisited.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He then mentioned that in the manifesto, they took a philosophical position.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But I am sorry because I still do not know what WP's position is.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, could the Leader of the Opposition clarify?

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Is he saying today that the EIP should be abolished?

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Is the answer to that, yes or no?

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Or is he saying that it need not be abolished, we can just look to see how we improve it?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Well, it is a very nice way to close off our discussion on this topic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I will be happy to clarify the doubts of the Leader of the House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The philosophical position remains, we aim as a society towards race neutrality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It does not matter what the colour of your skin is, we respect each other as Singaporeans, the Singapore family is going beyond CMIO categorisations and that is the target we need to keep in mind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That is where we want to endeavour towards.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Government is the government of the day, it wants to retain the EIP for reasons which I would say are not totally illegitimate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think it is important that I state that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But having said that, how do we move forward with the EIP as it is, knowing that there are minorities, knowing that there are minority communities, knowing that there are even majority, even the Chinese community, who are affected by it?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that is our duty as an opposition also.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Half the reason why I am asking for all that data on a neighbourhood-by-neighbourhood basis, over time – annually, not monthly – annually, is to try and see, for those neighbourhoods where EIP limits have been breached, what is unique about those neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is it very different from any other neighbourhood in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: How do we look into those details with more granularity?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I hope that clarifies the point by the Leader, but I do not think so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Both, indeed, the Workers' Party and we, agree we do want a race-neutral society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We want to raise a society where everybody can live happily together.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is a question of how do we get there.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And one of the things that the People's Action Party Government has put in place is the EIP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Pritam Singh comes to Parliament today and says revisit, review underlying philosophy and a few other things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I just want to know, today, is the Workers' Party saying we should remove the EIP?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If you are saying that we should do that, say so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the other hand, if you are saying, keep the EIP but let us improve it and ameliorate the impact on minorities, say so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, I think we know where we both stand and where we are in agreement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We still aim to remove it but, until we get there, we have to, as Minister said, even out the rough edges as much as possible and, at some point, I hope my generation, within our generation, we reach that place where we are race-neutral.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It does not mean that sometimes things do not bubble over.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But there are more important things that remind us that we are Singaporeans and we ought to look beyond our skin colour.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, that is a clear change in political position and I thank the Member for that.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My supplementary question actually takes the focus away from the EIP.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Minister referenced the Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) programme that is being taught in the schools right now.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I remember, not just from the Minister's point, but in the Committee of Supply earlier this year, there was due to be a review of the CCE.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, my supplementary question is actually for the Minister for Education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the review of the CCE, could the Minister share more details how we intend to incorporate the topics of multi-racialism and multiculturalism into the CCE syllabus and also how the syllabus will possibly be taught across the various platforms than we allow for a more vigorous, broader, intense debate?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My second question is, will the Ministry be looking into, say, for example, certain schools, where perhaps the student demographics are a little bit more homogeneous?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am not just talking about, say, SAP schools or madrasahs, but even certain schools which might be devoid of particular ethnicities for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And will the Ministry then perhaps adjust or tweak the CCE to cater to teaching the topics of multiculturalism and multi-racialism in these schools?

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The last review, as the Member is aware, began in 2018.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: So, as part of the review, besides drawing from the research on Character and Citizenship Education (CCE), we interacted with experts and practitioners on current and emerging trends, engaged community partners and stakeholders, such as school leaders, educators and students across all levels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: So, we continue to review CCE education, a very important part of our curriculum development for our students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This is done through engaging pedagogies that encourage students to voice out and explore the multiple perspectives, including the national perspective, and bearing in mind the common good.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: So, we are using different pedagogies and not just top-down, not just telling them what it is, to allow them to use experiential learning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: There is also a difference between the formal curriculum and the informal curriculum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is not just in the classrooms but also through exposures like co-curricular activities (CCAs) as well as uniformed group interactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: So, even as the Member mentioned earlier, circumstances where there are students with different kinds of profiles, CCE is not just in the classrooms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It also takes place in experiences and platforms where students interact with one another.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: So, for example, in CCA, in national competitions, camps, leadership camps, students are exposed to other groups of students and they are able to interact with one another.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The CCE curriculum also takes the age-appropriate dimension.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: So, the Primary schools get a different level of content versus the secondary schools versus the junior colleges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We also ensure that we train our teachers and our new teachers to be ready and prepared to implement the new curriculum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The new teachers are provided with this programme called the "CCE in the Singapore context" and so they are trained to deliver the content.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Even existing teachers are also given opportunities to look at different pedagogies because we know that students are exposed to different content on social media and they use some of these contents using new pedagogies to excite the students and, at the same time, acknowledge the importance of engaging in discourse of this nature.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am really glad to see that there are increasing efforts to enhance coordination between agencies, as issues, such as the potential entrenchment of community within the rental flat paradigm, are complex and really will require a more nuanced and sustained approach, as well as adequate resources to see real outcomes over the longer term.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, given that home ownership is also closely related to other factors, such as employment and family structures, is there room for Project DIAN@M3 to be a sandbox for potential policy adjustments and what sort of community assets will be integrated, given that these involve multiple agencies?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And finally, I am sure many of us will be interested in understanding what sort of outcomes the Government is hoping to see from this and also the timeline.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, could the Minister of State please share when will Project Dian@M3 be rolled out?

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In essence, we will augment the efforts of the community partners and the agencies that we have built partnership with, so that Malay/Muslim families who live in rental flats are able to take part in programmes and also receive holistic support from the programmes that we have.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These include counselling programmes under MENDAKI SENSE, Bersamamu and Project ARIF undertaken via the focus areas of M3 and with the support of the volunteers.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: When we look at the integration of assets relating to Project DIAN@M3, we are looking at the institutions that we have as well as the people and the volunteers.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, for M3@Towns, we have about 500 volunteers who have come on board and this is also something that we want to train them.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In addition to that, we also have volunteers that come on board via other programmes, like programmes relating to how we support vulnerable individuals as well as families; as well as how we support mentoring among the youths where more than 1,000 volunteers have come on board for our youth mentoring programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For efforts like Fitrah, we have about 460 volunteers as at June this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mayor Mohd Fahmi Aliman is also looking at how we can increase a lot more volunteers for efforts relating to upskilling of our people.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: So, essentially, we are very happy that many more volunteers are coming on board.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These are Malay/Muslims who have been very successful in their own life, in their fields and they are able to contribute back to the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to work with them, together with all the other Malay/Muslim organisations and Project DIAN@M3 will integrate these community assets that we have to help families in rental flats holistically and inspire them to be homeowners.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: My question relates to financial planning and estate planning for Malay/Muslims.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I just have a few supplementary questions on it.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is not uncommon for estates that go to intestacy to lead to familial disputes over the allocation of assets.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Muslim estate planning, under the Faraidh laws, allows Muslims to plan for one-third of their assets.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Ministry consider compiling data on whether there is currently still a lack of clarity on the estate planning options available to Muslims in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And would the Ministry also consider programmes for older or more mature families, not just for newly wed couples or young couples, who may be less tech-savvy and not as easily accessible for institutions, such as mosques or MENDAKI to reach out to?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, the problem that I see, is not so much the lack of programmes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: First, how do we get these programmes to the people who need them most.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Sometimes, we have to be very creative, we have to find ways to make it attractive for them to come.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A group of lawyers under M3 (Lawyers at M3) came together and said they wanted to educate our community about the same issues that the Member has raised.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I said, "Go ahead, tell me what you want to do." But they knew that if they just did it themselves, call it LPA, call it Faraidh, I do not think anyone would turn up.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But what they did instead was, they brought in an ustaz, a religious teacher, they brought in a popular personality and an artiste.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They put together a panel and said, "Come and talk to us".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We had to keep putting in chairs because people were still coming in to see what this was about.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At the same time, these lawyers also agreed to stay back after the programme, in case there were still questions that need to be answered.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Although some of the questions raised were really heart-wrenching, they were addressed in a very proper and enlightening way.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At the end of the session, because the lawyers agreed to stay back to hear other issues, there were long queues because people do have issues to clarify.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We do really need to do more of such programmes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We call upon our successful lawyers who have done this or have done this successfully, to come forward again.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: After we lift the restrictions for gatherings that we cannot now have because of COVID-19, we can have more of this.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I have two supplementary questions to the answer to my question.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: But we take every case that has been brought to the attention of the institutions very seriously, whether it is in the school or whether it is in the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Every report or every feedback given will be investigated thoroughly.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: As I mentioned in my earlier response, we will provide every opportunity for students to raise their concerns through various channels.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Every institution and school will have its own mechanism to investigate and we will take action against those found guilty of the alleged offences.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: The second question on whether programmes are differentiated, yes, I have mentioned earlier, in the schools, students can report to the leaders of the school, their teachers, any staff member that they are comfortable with.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In the IHLs, including the Polytechnics and ITE, there are various channels that the students are able to access.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Given what we have seen, especially in recent weeks, do we need to substantially tighten our laws or even introduce new rules to deal with racial outbursts and discrimination?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Two, I hear the Minister's points on CCA and social mixing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: During Committee of Supply 2021, I spoke on the need for more inter-school mixing through arts, culture and sports programmes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is especially so for missionary, madrasahs and the culturally oriented schools.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Does the Ministry plan to expand the current CCA or Youth Sports framework under SportSG and MOE?

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I have said in my speech earlier, where needed, action has been taken and I cited some examples.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Most recently, of course, there was an occasion where action was taken on the basis of breach of public nuisance.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Member will also know that we have the MRHA framework which I also alluded to.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What is useful about this framework, of course, is that it provides the outer parameters, defines the framework.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Which is sometimes the usefulness of having laws which define the parameters, especially when it comes to race and religious harmony, and issues surrounding community harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also will occasionally come across differences; there will be flash points from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The trick is to deal with this constructively, not try and stoke emotions in such already tensed situations, learn the differences.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I cannot pretend that we will always get along but the key to it is to try and find common ground.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And the way to find common ground is to try and assert less personal space, less of a "me-first" mentality.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I think when we do that, we will find that there will be a lot more space where we can do these exchanges.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: As a context, Mr Speaker, I think the Member would also appreciate that the madrasahs are not part of the national MOE education system; they are a separate education system, they are treated as a private education institution.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, they are not bound by the inter-school framework.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: On whether we should encourage that or not, I think we have to study that very carefully.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: But today, there are already opportunities for the madrasah students to interact with many of our national school students through various opportunities.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: For example, we have SAP schools like River Valley High working very closely with some of the madrasahs.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: The most important thing is that we want to find common spaces for our students and our young people to interact in the light of our conversation today, to facilitate greater inter-ethnic understanding.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Although they are in separate institutions, we should continue to find opportunities for them to interact, not just through inter-school games or inter-school CCAs but also other opportunities.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I remember when I was the Mayor of South East District, the Community Development Councils organise platforms like the Common Senses for Common Spaces, where students from different institutions come together to learn more about inter-religious understanding.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We can explore further opportunities for our young people to continue to interact regardless of where they are studying and, more importantly, to ensure that we try to expand the common spaces as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the light of this, can I ask our MCCY Minister, Mr Edwin Tong, to share with us the relevance of CMIO today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I just did a quick look; this last Sitting, we have seven or eight such PQs and they range from issues such as education, like Ms Raeesah Khan asked a question for tomorrow whether there are, and I quote, "any immediate and specific action plans to tackle the issue of low education levels of the Malay community".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: She has also asked another question for tomorrow where she has asked the Minister in charge of Muslim Affairs, "for each year from 2011 to 2020, how many Malays entered the local Universities and what is the percentage breakdown as compared to other races?" Mr Faisal Manap has also asked the question, I think, in writing, asking the Minister for Home Affairs what is the number of reports made by victims of sexual assault, asking for a breakdown by race.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Leon Perera, at an earlier Sitting, asked for MOH's Screen for Life programme to be broken down by ethnic lines.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think Ms He Ting Ru asked the same question for the breakdown in relation to elections.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the contrary, I think these are very important questions and it is not wrong to do so, and we agree.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The relevant Ministries will answer those questions fully.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The point though of citing these PQs is to say that, in reality, both sides of the House, and I think certainly on these examples, WP as well, realise that it is important to look at these outcomes by segments of society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And it is only if you have the CMIO classification and breakdown that you will be able to track performance of relative segments of society, to gauge the outcomes and to gauge for ourselves the efficacy and outcomes of these programmes that we have in place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This gives us, Mr Speaker, a good gauge of not just the relative performance of the segments in our society but also on the efficacy of our programmes and allows us to look at relative outcomes to assess where there might be gaps and to help in targeted, specialised, curated ways.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, Sir, with reference to the point made by the Member Mr Sitoh, I think these are important classifications that feed into an important outcome in terms of the programmes that we make.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I would invite the Workers' Party to consider this position and perhaps to state whether or not they see the CMIO as a relevant consideration today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I would suggest, Mr Speaker, that certainly from the nature, type and range of questions that they have asked in Parliament, I think that would appear to be so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I should thank Mr Sitoh for asking a question on our behalf.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think we have to accept that we operate on terms dictated by the Government which wins the mandate at the elections, and that has been the PAP government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think where we are coming from is – and I believe the Government is on the same page in this regard – that we want to level everybody up so that no race feels that the government policy does not reach out to them in a way which brings us to that destination which the Workers' Party wants Singapore to reach, of a race-neutral society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, these questions inevitably will be asked but the point I want to share with Minister Edwin Tong is, to what end do we keep asking these questions?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We want a situation where we can tell that government policy is improving outcomes, especially for communities which are not doing well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But let us be clear about where we want to go with this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister did not address the PQs I have filed for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: They are Written PQs, they are on the basis of the census that has been released last month.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Just to pick up on his last comment, to look at the outcomes and to see whether or not we can improve certain segments in society in Singapore and to look at whether the programmes help to uplift them, would he not accept that if you are looking at how to uplift certain segments by race, which we have done, then, would that not mean that the CMIO classification would not only be relevant, it would in fact be necessary to retain this distinction; at least for now, until we reach post-race-blind or race-neutral society?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think I can agree with the eventual outcome that even the Minister shares, which is to reach that race-neutral, race-blind end.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think you have to look at how the Government is performing on these indicators and eventually, with more Opposition Members in the House, looking at these numbers and figures, and asking more pointed questions and even putting up alternatives for debate and discussion, hopefully, we can reach that end state, which will be beneficial for all Singaporeans, not just this generation but those that come after us.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Or whether we should take what he calls a pre-emptive but the measures that we are taking today, to avoid such a situation arising?

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, are we more likely to arrive at a situation where Singaporeans learn to live with each other on a daily basis by making sure that we live in an integrated way on a daily basis in our estates?

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Or are we more likely to do so if we allow Singaporeans to live in segregated estates?

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And also, are we more likely to level everyone up if we are able to identify the issues that each of the communities in Singapore may face and therefore have more targeted programmes for them?

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Leader of the Opposition says we should be race-blind or race-neutral and just treat everybody as though they are exactly the same.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And then, are we likely to arrive at a good solution, where we reach this eventual outcome?

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Or are we less likely to do so?

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to ask the Leader of the Opposition whether he agrees with me, because he mentioned more Members of Opposition in the House would lead to better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is the Senior Minister suggesting that the WP is using these episodes for political purposes?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The answer is no, we do not do that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I appreciate the accolade because I think it is appropriate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In terms of the series of hypotheticals that the Senior Minister put out, I think moving from one extreme to another extreme is probably not the policy approach; hence, the earlier exchange we had about evolving the EIP to suit the needs of this current generation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I hope it does not undermine or take away the point that philosophically, where does the WP want Singapore to go?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I do not think the PAP is very far away from this – that we all are trying to move towards a race-neutral society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We may have different approaches of going at it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We, of course, have the harder job of trying to second guess what is reasonable in the way we move there, because we do not have the information and the broad sweep of facts that the Government has.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I think, by and large, we accept that we have to move forward in a way where Singapore, as a country, as a society, is strengthened.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think even the WP agrees on that; the Leader of the Opposition says so too.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Are we more likely to achieve an integrated Singapore by having integrated housing or to abolish the EIP as the WP would propose today and have segregated housing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And then, how do we learn how to live together again?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am glad to hear the Leader of the Opposition say that we should all not exploit the issues of race and religion for political purposes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), Written Answers to Question Nos 22-33, 35-38, 40, 42, 47-48, 54-58, 60-64, 73-76, 78-96, 98-104, 106-111, 114-115 and 120 on the Order Paper are reproduced in the Appendix.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The remaining Questions have been postponed to a later Sitting of Parliament or withdrawn.]
